claims.text: Check attention first: inattention points to delirium.
claims.quote: Attention is assessed first. Inattention is most consistent with the diagnosis of delirium, although advanced dementia also severely impairs attention.
The Mini-Mental Status Examination (see sidebar Examination of Mental Status ) or the Montreal Cognitive Assessment (MoCA), is often used as a bedside screening test

claims.text: TSH and vit B12 for everyone.
claims.quote: Tests should include thyroid-stimulating hormone (TSH) and vitamin B12 levels.

claims.text: CBC, kidney and liver tests are sometimes recommended, but their yield = very ↓.
claims.quote: Routine complete blood count (CBC) and kidney and liver function tests are sometimes recommended, but their yield for identifying underlying disease is very low.

claims.text: HIV or syphilis testing when findings suggest it.
claims.quote: If clinical findings suggest a specific disorder, other tests (eg, for HIV or syphilis) are indicated.

claims.text: CT or MRI @ the initial eval and after any unexplained Δ in cognition.
claims.quote: CT or MRI should be done in the initial evaluation of dementia and after any unexplained change in cognition or mental status.

claims.text: Lumbar puncture for sus chronic infect or neurosyphilis, or rapidly progress dementia (prion or autoimmune dz).
claims.quote: Lumbar puncture should be considered if chronic infection or neurosyphilis is suspected or in patients with a rapidly progressive dementia to evaluate for possible prion disease or an autoimmune disorder.

claims.text: Neuropsychological testing when Hx and bedside testing are ⍉conclusive.
claims.quote: Neuropsychologic testing should be done when history and bedside mental status testing are not conclusive.
Routine genetic testing for the presence of epsilon-4 alleles (ApoE4) is not recommended as part of the diagnostic work-up for dementia.

claims.text: Consider depression: depressed older pts tend to exaggerate their memory loss and rarely forget important current events.
claims.quote: Depressed older patients may experience cognitive decline, but unlike patients with dementia, they tend to exaggerate their memory loss and rarely forget important current events or personal matters.
